title: AP 3-D Art and Design
summary: Study mass, space, material behaviour and the evidence needed to present three-dimensional work.
frameworkNote: Checked against the official course page on 15 October 2026 for 2026-27. This is an original four-part portfolio skill sequence across inquiry, making and presentation, not prescribed College Board units. Text exercises support planning and reflection; they do not create, assess or certify a portfolio. Check current submission and AI rules with your teacher.

modules.title: Investigate occupied and empty space
modules.focus: Develop a spatial inquiry that needs more than one view.
explanation: Three-dimensional design organises volume and the space around or within it. A void can carry as much meaning as a solid mass. A tunnel, opening or repeated gap changes what a viewer can see and how the eye or body moves through the work.

Start from a question that requires spatial decisions, such as how a narrow opening can suggest protection and restriction at once. Make small safe models, turn them, and record how the relationship changes. A front photograph alone may hide the most important opening, so observation and documentation should include several angles.

workedExample.prompt: Investigate a shelter made from folded card.
steps: Make one model with a broad entrance and another with a narrow entrance.
Compare the interior view and surrounding negative space before choosing what to develop.

misconception.claim: Empty space is simply unused material.
misconception.correction: A deliberately shaped void is an active part of a spatial composition.

questions.prompt: How could a hollow form communicate fragility?
questions.hint: Connect an opening to the remaining structure.
questions.answer: Large openings and thin connecting walls can make support visibly delicate, provided the model remains safely stable.
checkpoints: Names a spatial choice
Connects form to meaning

questions.prompt: Why compare the side and front views?
questions.answer: A solid-looking front may conceal a hollow interior or uneven balance visible from the side.
checkpoints: Explains changing evidence
Uses more than one viewpoint

questions.prompt: How could a sculpture suggest exclusion without using a literal locked door?
questions.answer: A low opening could prevent entry into a larger visible interior. The contrast makes access seem unequal. Multiple views should preserve that relation rather than conceal it.
checkpoints: A low opening could prevent entry into a larger visible interior.
The contrast makes access seem unequal.

questions.prompt: Why test a wearable sculpture on a scaled model before full construction?
hints: Connect the test to the inquiry.
questions.answer: A model reveals proportions and possible restrictions. It helps test how the form relates to a body. Those observations can guide a safer, more purposeful full-scale design.
checkpoints: A model reveals proportions and possible restrictions.
It helps test how the form relates to a body.
Those observations can guide a safer, more purposeful full-scale design.

notes.title: Investigate occupied and empty space in depth
paragraphs: Three-dimensional inquiry involves occupied volume, surrounding space and the viewer's possible movement. A void is an active relationship between surfaces, not merely unused material. Compare openings from multiple viewpoints: an opening visible from the front may disappear as the viewer moves. Scale also changes bodily relationships, including whether a form can be held, approached or entered. A spatial inquiry should need those relationships to communicate its idea. Photographs can support analysis, but a single view may hide the most important interaction.

workedExamples.prompt: Explore enclosure with two curved card walls.
steps: Place them close together to make a narrow passage, then widen the gap while keeping their height.
View the passage from its entrance and side to compare invitation with restriction.
workedExamples.conclusion: The gap, rather than the amount of card, becomes the main variable shaping enclosure.

flashcards.front: Can a void carry an idea?
flashcards.back: Yes; its shape can imply access or restriction.

modules.title: Test structure and material behaviour
modules.focus: Choose joints and supports that serve the form.
explanation: A material has properties as well as associations. Card folds, wire bends and clay changes as it dries. The connection between parts affects both structural reliability and appearance. Plan safe tools and teacher-supervised processes appropriate to the material before working.

A model that stands still can still be unstable if its centre of mass lies near the edge of its support area. Test small versions on a level surface and document how added height or an overhang changes balance. Artistic tension can be suggested through form without making a dangerous object.

workedExample.prompt: A tall card tower leans after an upper platform is attached.
steps: Locate how the platform shifts weight toward one side.
Widen the base or reposition the platform, then compare stability and the intended silhouette.

misconception.claim: If a sculpture stands once, its structure is resolved.
misconception.correction: Stability depends on support, joints and expected handling conditions, not one photograph.

questions.prompt: Why test a joint before making the full work?
questions.answer: A small test shows whether the joint holds the chosen materials and whether its appearance fits the work.
checkpoints: Tests structure
Tests visual consequence

questions.prompt: How can visible bracing support an inquiry about dependence?
questions.hint: Treat support as a visual element.
questions.answer: Repeated braces can reveal how each section relies on another, making structural support part of the idea.
checkpoints: Links process to idea
Names a visible relationship

questions.prompt: A glued joint fails at the join between smooth plastic and card. What should the next experiment isolate?
questions.answer: Test suitable surface preparation or mechanical fastening on small samples. Keep the materials and load comparable. Record both holding strength and the joint's appearance.
checkpoints: Test suitable surface preparation or mechanical fastening on small samples.
Keep the materials and load comparable.
Record both holding strength and the joint's appearance.

questions.prompt: Why can simply adding more mass to a leaning sculpture worsen the problem?
hints: Consider its relation to the support.
questions.answer: Mass added on the leaning side increases imbalance. Its position matters as much as its amount. Repositioning the mass or support may better preserve the form.
checkpoints: Mass added on the leaning side increases imbalance.
Its position matters as much as its amount.
Repositioning the mass or support may better preserve the form.

notes.title: Test structure and material behaviour in depth
paragraphs: Structure and expression interact when joints, supports and material behaviour remain visible. A form's stability depends on how its mass relates to its support and on the strength of connections. Materials may bend, compress or split differently, so a small joint test is useful before committing to a larger assembly. Evaluate the test both physically and visually. A concealed brace may preserve a smooth silhouette, while an exposed brace can make dependence or tension part of the meaning. Neither solution is automatically preferable.

workedExamples.prompt: A wire arch spreads at its feet when loaded with paper forms.
steps: Observe that the added load pushes the supports farther apart.
Test a connecting base tie and compare the resulting silhouette with a wider fixed base.
workedExamples.conclusion: The selected support should resist spreading while serving the intended visual relationship.

flashcards.front: What should a joint test assess?
flashcards.back: Strength and visual fit with the work.
It affects balance over the support.

modules.title: Revise scale, rhythm and surface
modules.focus: Change spatial relationships with a clear purpose.
explanation: Repetition creates rhythm across a structure, but exact repetition is only one possibility. Increasing gaps or changing the size of repeated units can direct a viewer around a form. Scale also changes how an object relates to a hand, room or body.

Surface and mass interact. A smooth surface can unify a fragmented form; a rough surface can interrupt a continuous volume. Compare changes in a model before committing to a final material. Record the original decision, the effect you observed and the revised relationship so that development remains visible.

workedExample.prompt: A ring of identical modules feels static.
steps: Keep the circular arrangement while gradually increasing the gaps.
Inspect whether the changing rhythm directs the eye, then revise one abrupt jump that distracts from the intended progression.

misconception.claim: Revision means covering mistakes with decoration.
misconception.correction: Revision may change proportion, space, structure or process rather than adding surface detail.

questions.prompt: How would doubling a wearable object’s scale change its meaning?
questions.hint: Consider its relationship to the body.
questions.answer: It may become restrictive or theatrical rather than practical; explain the effect using its actual position and weight.
checkpoints: Connects scale to experience
Avoids assuming one fixed meaning

questions.prompt: What evidence could show a rhythm revision?
questions.answer: Photograph two models from the same angle and annotate how changing intervals alters movement around the form.
checkpoints: Uses comparable views
Names the altered relationship

questions.prompt: A sculpture uses identical modules but feels monotonous. Suggest a purposeful revision without replacing the modules.
questions.hint: Change a relationship rather than the objects.
hints: Change a relationship rather than the objects.
questions.answer: Gradually rotate successive modules. The changing orientation creates directional movement. Compare whether that movement supports the intended idea.
checkpoints: Gradually rotate successive modules.
The changing orientation creates directional movement.

questions.prompt: Why should a reflective surface be tested in the intended display lighting?
questions.answer: Light and surroundings alter what the surface reflects. Glare may conceal form or create emphasis. The intended setting is needed to judge that effect.
checkpoints: Light and surroundings alter what the surface reflects.
Glare may conceal form or create emphasis.

notes.title: Revise scale, rhythm and surface in depth
paragraphs: Rhythm in spatial work develops through intervals, repetitions and changes encountered over time. Surface can reinforce or interrupt that rhythm: a glossy area may attract attention differently from a rough one. Altering scale changes more than size because weight, movement and the viewer's bodily relation may change too. Compare revisions from consistent viewpoints while also walking around the work. State which spatial relationship changed and whether the result supports the inquiry, rather than treating greater complexity as automatic improvement.

workedExamples.prompt: Revise a row of five suspended paper forms to suggest acceleration.
steps: Decrease the gaps progressively while keeping the forms' size constant.
Compare the direction of the tightening rhythm from both ends.
workedExamples.conclusion: Progressively compressed intervals can suggest acceleration, with viewing direction affecting the reading.

flashcards.back: Repeated forms and the intervals between them.
It makes the revision's effect easier to identify.

modules.title: Document a spatial work
modules.focus: Represent volume, scale and process accurately.
explanation: Documentation translates a physical work into images. Choose views that reveal mass, voids, surface and important connections. Consistent lighting helps viewers distinguish a shadow from a dark material. Include detail views only when they clarify something the overall view cannot show.

Dimensions and material descriptions establish scale more reliably than a dramatic camera angle. Preserve photographs of significant changes and identify what each one demonstrates. A strong presentation is selective but honest: do not use cropping or digital alteration to conceal a structural or material feature relevant to the work.

workedExample.prompt: Plan documentation for a hollow woven form.
steps: Use an overall three-quarter view to show volume and openings.
Add a detail of the weaving connection and a second view that reveals the interior; record dimensions and materials.

misconception.claim: One dramatic photograph is always sufficient.
misconception.correction: Spatial relationships often require several complementary views.

questions.prompt: Why might a low camera angle misrepresent a small model?
questions.answer: It can make the model appear monumental while hiding its actual scale and top surfaces.
checkpoints: Identifies distortion
Suggests dimensions or another view

questions.prompt: Write a concrete revision note for a widened base.
questions.answer: I widened the base to support the offset upper mass, keeping the asymmetry while reducing tipping.
checkpoints: Names the change
Explains its purpose

questions.prompt: A sculpture photograph hides its unstable rear support. Why is another view needed?
questions.answer: The hidden support affects the actual structure. A rear or side view makes that relationship visible. Accurate documentation should not imply unsupported stability.
checkpoints: The hidden support affects the actual structure.
A rear or side view makes that relationship visible.
Accurate documentation should not imply unsupported stability.

questions.prompt: Write a revision note for shortening an overhanging arm.
questions.answer: I shortened the overhang to reduce strain on the joint. I retained its offset position to preserve asymmetry. The revision balances structural support with the intended imbalance in appearance.
checkpoints: I shortened the overhang to reduce strain on the joint.
I retained its offset position to preserve asymmetry.
The revision balances structural support with the intended imbalance in appearance.

notes.title: Document a spatial work in depth
paragraphs: Spatial documentation translates a bodily encounter into selected views. Each image should contribute information: an overall view establishes volume, a second view reveals hidden relationships, and a detail explains a material or joint. Include dimensions and identify the orientation when it matters. Lighting should make surfaces legible without inventing a different structure through dramatic shadows. Process photographs can demonstrate a revision if the comparison keeps viewpoint and scale sufficiently consistent. Documentation is strongest when it represents the actual work accurately and explains why those views were selected.

workedExamples.prompt: Document a spiral made from joined cardboard strips.
steps: Use a three-quarter view showing depth and the central void.
Add a top view for the spiral's spacing and a detail of the join.
workedExamples.conclusion: Together, the views explain volume, interval and construction without relying on a single dramatic angle.

flashcards.back: The work's principal form and volume.
